Sturdy
STUR-dee
noun / verb (Gen Alpha slang)
From English sturdy (strong, firm, hardy). As slang, "hit the sturdy" names a stomping, knee-bouncing, shoulder-rocking dance from New York City — Bronx and Brooklyn — tied to the New York drill music scene of the early 2020s; it went viral in 2022–23 through street videos, NFL celebrations, and school hallways. Gen Alpha uses "hit the sturdy" for the dance and "sturdy" as praise for something tough or solid. Parents should know that much of the drill music the dance grew up with carries violent lyrics, while the dance itself does not.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

To hit the sturdy is to do a heavy, stomping, bouncing dance that started in New York. Gen Alpha kids do it to celebrate, and they also use "sturdy" the way grandparents did — for something strong that will not fall over. The Christian observation: the old word is the better word, and Scripture is full of the sturdy. The man who trusts God "shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water" (Psa 1:3). Paul’s command to a church sounds like a sturdy stance: "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong" (1Co 16:13), and to every believer: "be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might" (Eph 6:10). The strongest stance in the world is the one that stands on God: "he only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved" (Psa 62:6). The dance’s background in drill music is a reason for a parent to know what songs a child is hearing with it; the dance itself is a stomp of joy. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Sturdy means strong, like a tree that doesn’t fall down in the wind. When we hold on to Jesus, we’re sturdy inside — the wind can’t knock us over."

Webster 1828 Definition

New York stomping dance ("hit the sturdy," viral 2022–23) and praise-word for something tough — the old word for the strength Scripture locates in those who stand fast in the Lord.

STURDY, n. / v. (New York dance, viral 2022–present; Gen Alpha usage) A stomping, knee-bouncing celebration dance. "Hit the sturdy!"

Praise sense: tough, solid, impressive. "That shot was sturdy."

Background: New York drill music scene, early 2020s.

Decode for parents: the dance is fine; know the songs it travels with.

Webster 1828, the root — STURDY, a. Hardy; stout; foolishly obstinate; implying coarseness or rudeness.

Key Scripture

Psa 1:3 — "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper."

1Co 16:13 — "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong."

Eph 6:10 — "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might."

Psa 62:6 — "He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved."

Modern Corruption

The sturdy dance is a harmless stomp; the word’s real strength is the old one Scripture gives to those who stand fast in the faith and are not moved.

expand to see more

The dance carries a soundtrack. New York drill, the scene that gave it its home, is notorious for lyrics about violence and rivalry, and a child who learns a dance from a video often learns the song too. That is the only real caution, and it is a caution about music more than movement.

The word is a gift. Teach your child that sturdy is what God makes His people: rooted like the tree of Psalm 1, standing fast like Paul’s church, strong in the Lord. Then let him stomp.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French estourdi (stunned, reckless) → English sturdy (strong, firm) → New York "hit the sturdy" dance (2022–23).

expand to see more

Old French estourdi — stunned, violent, reckless

Middle English sturdi — fierce; later, strong and firm

Early 2020s: New York drill scene; "hit the sturdy"

2022–23: viral in street videos, NFL celebrations, school hallways

Usage

""We won the relay and everybody hit the sturdy.""

"Stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong — that’s sturdy (1Co 16:13)."
